analysis.one_liner: Speeds federal permitting for energy projects, shifts drilling oversight to states, and mandates the Mountain Valley Pipeline with no court review.
analysis.headline: 46 of 50 Senate Republicans cosponsored the bill, but the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee never acted on it, and it died when the 117th Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: The START Act would rewrite how the federal government reviews energy projects — pipelines, power plants, drilling, and transmission lines. It would impose deadlines meant to finish permits quickly, cap the length of environmental impact statements at 200 pages, and give lawsuits against energy permits a strict 60-day filing window. It would also lock in Trump-era environmental rules, let states take over fracking regulation and even energy leasing on federal land without federal environmental review, stop agencies from using estimates of the dollar cost of greenhouse gas emissions, and single out one project: the Mountain Valley Pipeline, whose permits and approvals it would force through within 21 days, shielded from any court challenge [S3]. The bill never left committee [S5].
analysis.who_benefits: Oil and gas companies and pipeline developers, above all the backers of the Mountain Valley Pipeline. Energy developers generally — including those building transmission lines — would also gain from faster permitting and a shorter window for legal challenges to their projects.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Oil and gas and pipeline developers

how_it_helps.text: It requires every federal agency authorization needed to build an energy project to be decided within 90 days after the lead agency issues its final decision, and sets an overall two-year target for the entire environmental review and permitting process [S3].

It caps the text of an environmental impact statement for an energy project at roughly 200 pages and lets agencies borrow each other's 'categorical exclusions' — categories of projects exempted from detailed review entirely [S3].
It gives challenges to energy project permits a 60-day filing deadline and bars lawsuits filed later, shortening the period in which opponents can go to court [S3].

It gives states sole authority over fracking regulation, including on federal land within the state, and lets any state take over leasing, permitting, and regulation of energy development on federal land in place of the federal government — with those state decisions exempt from the Administrative Procedure Act, the Endangered Species Act, and the National Environmental Policy Act [S3].

It orders the Army, Agriculture, and Interior departments to issue every remaining approval for the Mountain Valley Pipeline within 21 days of enactment, exempts those approvals from judicial review, and preempts any law or court decision that would block them [S3].

It codifies the 2020 Trump administration NEPA regulations and the January 2021 narrower definition of 'waters of the United States' into law, so a future administration could not simply undo them by rewriting regulations [S3].

analysis.who_pays: People who live near pipelines, wells, and other energy projects — including the landowners along the Mountain Valley Pipeline route — would lose their strongest tools for challenging projects, since lawsuits would face a 60-day deadline and the pipeline's approvals could not be challenged at all. The public would also lose federal environmental review where a state takes over development on federal land, and agencies could no longer count the dollar cost of greenhouse gas emissions when writing rules.
analysis.who_pays_short: Communities near energy projects and landowners

drawbacks.text: It removes judicial review entirely for the Mountain Valley Pipeline's approvals and exempts state-permitted energy development on federal land from the Endangered Species Act and the National Environmental Policy Act, leaving affected communities and tribes few ways to challenge projects that affect their land and water [S3].

The 60-day deadline for lawsuits against energy permits can expire before harm from a project is apparent, and suits filed later would be barred — a threshold most affected residents could not realistically meet [S3].

It bans federal agencies from using any social cost of greenhouse gas estimate in rulemaking, so the climate and health damages of emissions would not be weighed against the benefits of the rules those agencies write [S3].

The strongest good-faith case for the bill: environmental review of major infrastructure often drags on for many years, and supporters argued that firm deadlines, shorter statements, and a defined window for litigation would cut costs and delays that also slow renewable energy and transmission projects. That benefit is real, but this bill bundles it with carve-outs that would gut review for fossil fuel projects and mandate one specific pipeline [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Faster and more predictable permitting is a legitimate goal that would help some clean energy and transmission projects too. But the bill is lopsided: it pairs modest streamlining with sweeping exemptions — states taking over federal land development free of federal environmental law, a total bar on court review of one pipeline, and a ban on counting climate damages in rulemaking — that fall almost entirely to the benefit of fossil fuel developers and to the cost of the people who live around their projects [S3].

outcome.mechanism: The Senate referred it to the Environment and Public Works Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never held a hearing or vote, and the bill expired when the Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: Senator Shelley Moore Capito introduced the START Act on September 12, 2022, with Senate Republican Leader Mitch McConnell among the original cosponsors [S1].
All 46 cosponsors were Republicans — 46 of the Senate's 50 — and no Democrat joined [S4].
The bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Environment and Public Works the day it was introduced; the action record shows no hearing, no markup, and no floor vote afterward [S5].
The CRS summary describes it as a bill to expedite the environmental review of energy projects, 'such as the Mountain Valley Pipeline project' [S2].
The 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023, and the bill died in committee [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The bill's death left existing environmental review rules in place, so oil and gas companies and the Mountain Valley Pipeline's backers did not get the carve-outs they sought. That may have been a matter of the calendar as much as opposition: the bill arrived with just weeks left in a session dominated by other fights, with only its sponsoring party behind it.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Existing environmental rules and nearby communities

for.name: Sen. Shelley Moore Capito
for.role: U.S. Senator from West Virginia (lead sponsor)
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and gathered cosponsors; its state-control and pipeline provisions tracked the interests of her state's natural gas industry.

for.name: 46 of 50 Senate Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including Minority Leader Mitch McConnell; no Democrat did.

against.name: Sen. Tom Carper
against.role: Chair, Senate Environment and Public Works Committee
against.what_they_did: Chaired the committee the bill was referred to; the record shows no hearing, markup, or vote was ever scheduled on it.

sides.party_line_note: Every cosponsor was a Republican — 46 of the 50 Senate Republicans, plus Capito herself — and no Democrat signed on; with Democrats holding the committee chair and the chamber's agenda, the bill never advanced.

industries.note: The bill names this one project and orders three cabinet departments to issue every remaining approval within 21 days, with no possibility of a court challenge — a favor no other project in the country received.

States could take over energy development on federal land free of federal environmental review, fracking would be regulated solely by states (even on federal land), a narrower definition of protected waters would be locked in, and discharge permits would run 10 years instead of 5.

industries.industry: Owners of existing fossil-fired power plants and industrial emitters
industries.note: A redefinition of 'modification' under the Clean Air Act would let plants make efficiency, reliability, and safety upgrades without triggering New Source Review permitting, even where achievable hourly emissions could rise.

industries.industry: Energy project developers generally, including transmission and renewables
industries.note: The permitting deadlines, two-year review target, and shorter EISs would apply to all energy projects, which could speed transmission lines and other clean energy buildout — though the same bill locks in Trump-era NEPA rules and bans the use of greenhouse gas cost estimates.
